Hello! I'm working on formalizing domain theory for my final project in Brown University's Formal Proof and Verification course, following Abramsky-Jung handbook. I have a question about CompletePartialOrder (Mathlib.Order.CompletePartialOrder). I noticed that we can prove that any CompletePartialOrder has a unique bottom element:

lemma complete_partial_order_has_bottom {α : Type*} [CompletePartialOrder α] : ∃ x : α, IsBot x := by
  have h₁ : DirectedOn (· ≤ ·) (∅ : Set α) := by
    rw [DirectedOn]
    simp
  have h₂: IsLUB ∅ (sSup ∅) := CompletePartialOrder.lubOfDirected ∅ h₁
  use sSup ∅
  rw [IsLUB, IsLeast, upperBounds, lowerBounds] at h₂
  simp at h₂
  exact h₂

Thus, should we add an instance CompletePartialOrder.toOrderBot? I noticed that in some domain theory literature (e.g., the handbook), directed sets are required to be non-empty. Under this alternative definition, a directed-complete partial order wouldn't necessarily have a bottom element, which makes it a more general structure.

Addtionally, I've also formalized several key concepts from the handbook:

  • Way-below relation (Definition 2.2.1)
  • Continuous directed-complete partial order (Definition 2.2.6)
  • Scott topology on continuous directed-complete partial order (Proposition 2.3.6)
  • Existence of fixpoint for Scott continuous functions (Theorem 2.1.19.1)

Would you be interested in these? I'd be happy to contribute them to Mathlib.
(docs#CompletePartialOrder, docs#DirectedOn for reference)

So I guess your proposal is changing CompletePartialOrder to have the field

 lubOfDirected (d : Set α) :
-  DirectedOn (· ≤ ·) d → IsLUB d (sSup d)
+  Nonempty d → DirectedOn (· ≤ ·) d → IsLUB d (sSup d)

+  Nonempty d → DirectedOn (fun (x1 x2 : α) => x1 ≤ x2) d → IsLUB d (sSup d)

Christopher Hoskin said:

I was working initially from Gierz et al where directed sets are also required to be non-empty. This required havingd.Nonempty → DirectedOn (· ≤ ·) d → everywhere in #2508.

That's true! In my formalization, d.Nonempty → DirectedOn (· ≤ ·) d → appears almost everywhere, which is a bit annoying. I have two proposals:
Adding CompletePartialOrder.toOrderBot and keeping the definition of CompletePartialOrder unchanged

instance CompletePartialOrder.toOrderBot {α : Type*} [CompletePartialOrder α] : OrderBot α where
  bot := sSup ∅
  bot_le := by
    have h₁: DirectedOn (· ≤ ·) (∅ : Set α) := by
      simp [DirectedOn]
    have h₂: IsLUB ∅ (sSup ∅) := CompletePartialOrder.lubOfDirected ∅ h₁
    simp [IsLUB, IsLeast, upperBounds, lowerBounds] at h₂
    exact h₂

Or changing the definition of CompletePartialOrder and adding a typeclass PointedCompletePartialOrder (we still need to write d.Nonempty → DirectedOn (· ≤ ·) d →)

 lubOfDirected (d : Set α) :
-  DirectedOn (· ≤ ·) d → IsLUB d (sSup d)
+  d.Nonempty  → DirectedOn (· ≤ ·)  d → IsLUB d (sSup d)

class PointedCompletePartialOrder (α : Type*) extends CompletePartialOrder α, OrderBot α

Which one do we prefer?
What about the third option of simply making CompletePartialOrder extend OrderBot?

I would imagine that if a concrete type implements CompletePartialOrder, then it's likely to also implement OrderBot. Adding the instance CompletePartialOrder.toOrderBot manually can potentially create diamonds.
If it's useful, we can define a constructor for CompletePartialOrder which takes in the other properties and fills in bot = sSup Ø.

I think the two reasonable options here are to either extend OrderBot as Violeta says, or to restrict the axioms such that it is not implied at all (and the choice between these is a mathematical / terminology one). Indeed, bot := sSup Ø will create instance diamonds.

If we let CompletePartialOrder extend OrderBot:

class CompletePartialOrder (α: Type*) extends PartialOrder α, SupSet α, OrderBot α where
  lubOfDirected : ∀ d, DirectedOn (· ≤ ·) d → IsLUB d (sSup d)

I think a construtor like this might be helpful:

noncomputable def mkCompletePartialOrder {α : Type*}
  [PartialOrder α] [OrderBot α] (sSup : Set α → α)
  (lubOfDirected : ∀ d, d.Nonempty → DirectedOn (· ≤ ·) d → IsLUB d (sSup d)) :
  CompletePartialOrder α where
  sSup := by
    intro d
    by_cases d.Nonempty
    · exact sSup d
    · exact ⊥
  lubOfDirected := by
    intro d
    by_cases h : d.Nonempty
    · simp [h]
      exact lubOfDirected d h
    · simp [Set.not_nonempty_iff_eq_empty.mp h]

I would imagine we typically assume we're working with nonempty sets, when discussing LUB.

Here, we get both the flexibility of talking about the potentially empty notion with docs#PreconnectedSpace (which we currently get with docs#Directed) but simultaneously talking about the usual notion with docs#ConnectedSpace (which we currently don't have a name for).

The clear cut, in this case, is every complaint in this and other threads about painpoints when we unfold the definition.
The literature definition gives an elimination rule:

"If (≼ preorder), (∀ x y : s ∃ z : s x ≼ z ≽ y), (s.Nonempty) ⊢ ϕ,
then s directeds \,\mathrm{directed}sdirected ⊢ ϕ"

and when the literature says "for all directed sets s, P s, it is almost invariably in a setting where ≼ is a preorder.

Then when someone tries to encode such a statement from the literature,
— e.g. docs#Topology.scottHausdorff , docs#ScottContinuousOn , docs#DirSupClosed
docs#CondtionallyCompletePartialOrderSup —
writing s → Directed s → P s encodes the wrong thing, even in the presence of a Preorder α. This is because the actual elimination rule is

"If (≼ preorder), (∀ x y : s ∃ z : s x ≼ z ≽ y) ⊢ ϕ,
then DirectedOn (. ≼ .) s ⊢ ϕ"

it's genuinely unclear whether docs#CompletePartialOrder was an esoteric naming of DCPO that made such a mistake, or the common naming of CPO. This is bad! Formalization mistakes of this class should not be possible ambiguous for such an agreed upon term!
I am far too milquetoast to copy Kevin's language of "disastrous", but it is certainly not ideal

why aren't we slippery sloped into adding IsPreorder ? Because in ≥99% of the places people formalize a statement that eliminates over directed sets, the statement is already parameterised with a preordered set. Nothing is broken by the absence of this assumption
(whereas everyone trying to get formalisation done with directed sets is constantly tripping over the absence of Nonempty)

[TL; DR]: instead of treating Nonempty vs Preorder an [analytic philosophy / normative linguistics] distinction, treat it as a UX distinction.
The UX concern is not "mixin bloat". The UX concern is it increases the risk of honest mistakes

A biased overview of Domain Theory

Domain theory is "order theory for people who really care about (co)recursion and (co)induction". It is the foundation for doing docs#Std.Do.WP, or fixpoints of polynomial functors, in anything outside deterministic monads. Any algorithm morally in BPP or bounded quantifier form often has semantics best expressed using domain theory as a foundation.
@Jireh Loreaux's example of weak\* operator topologies on C algebras closely resembles literature attempts at denotational semantics for "quantum" Hoare logics.
In another phrasing, domain theory is topological order theory for people who mostly only care about the Scott and Lawson topologies (plus the generic patch/prod/pi/sum/etc constructions)

(EDIT: 3:00am exposition on MonadRandom)

and many of the standard definitions — not just results, but definitions — use "directed" while talking about a pre or partial order

This is a large body of theory relevant to, at minimum, mathlib and cslib, if not eventually Std's MonadRandom / MonadNondet / Monad[...] instances, that is very easy to formalise wrong because of Directed

and biased / contentiously,

for cslib in particular, any application of order theory that isn't docs#WellFounded is very likely to use either NonemptyChain or Nonempty ∩ Directed as the minimal assumptions.
Flippantly, Domain Theory is the result of people in the 70s onwards looking at Knaster-Tarski and Bourbaki-Witt and trying to generalise for computer science use cases
it is not at risk from the absence of Preorder
